findings.explanation: This module's entire premise (README: "add your users to the ssh users group") is that group membership grants access to the bastion. But the inline policy's Resource is `arn:aws:ec2:${var.region}:${var.account_id}:instance/*` — a wildcard scoped only by region and account, matching every EC2 instance in the account, not the bastion specifically. A deterministic rule can't catch this: HLD_AWS_222 (no-wildcard-resource) only matches a literal `"*"` element, and `instance/*` is a syntactically valid, non-wildcard-literal ARN string that requires knowing AWS ARN semantics to recognise as "all instances." Any member of the ssh group (or anyone who compromises one) can use ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey to push a key onto any other instance in the account running an `ec2-user` OS account — turning a bastion-scoped access group into an account-wide lateral SSH path.
findings.remediation: Scope the Resource/Condition to only the bastion's instances. The ASG now tags launched instances with `Name = var.name` (see aws_autoscaling_group.bastion.tf), so add a Condition such as `"ec2:ResourceTag/Name": var.name` to the statement, or narrow Resource beyond `instance/*` if a fixed set of instance ARNs is acceptable. Verify EC2 Instance Connect actually honours the `aws:ResourceTag` condition key for this action before relying on it.
findings.resolution_note: Resource stays instance/* (ASG instance IDs are dynamic, unknowable at policy-authoring time), but added `"aws:ResourceTag/Name": "${var.name}"` to the existing Condition StringEquals block in aws_iam_group.ssh.tf. Only instances tagged Name = var.name (i.e. the bastion's own ASG-launched instances) satisfy the condition, so SendSSHPublicKey no longer reaches arbitrary account instances.
findings.title: "ssh" IAM group can push SSH keys to every EC2 instance in the account, not just the bastion

findings.explanation: The role is used purely as an EC2 instance profile: the SSM agent running on the instance authenticates via the instance profile automatically (through IMDS), and the only policy attached (var.ssm_standard_role, default AmazonEC2RoleforSSM) is the standard instance-role policy. Trusting `ssm.amazonaws.com` to independently call sts:AssumeRole on this role is only needed for specific SSM features (e.g. cross-account Automation or hybrid activations) that this module does not use. This is a judgment call the engine can't make — it would need to know that the attached policy is the standard agent policy and infer the trust relationship is broader than that use case requires.
findings.remediation: If no SSM feature in this account depends on the service assuming this specific role, drop `ssm.amazonaws.com` from the assume-role principals in data.iam_policy_document.tf and keep only `ec2.amazonaws.com`.
findings.resolution_note: Dropped ssm.amazonaws.com from the principals block in data.iam_policy_document.tf, leaving only ec2.amazonaws.com, matching AWS's documented trust policy for an SSM-managed EC2 instance profile role. Left a comment explaining why and noting the CloudTrail/Access-Analyzer check to re-verify if a future SSM feature needs it back.
findings.title: IAM role trust policy allows ssm.amazonaws.com to assume the role directly, which standard SSM agent operation does not require

findings.explanation: AWS deprecated AmazonEC2RoleforSSM in favour of AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, a narrower, purpose-built policy for the SSM agent; AWS's own guidance is to not use the legacy policy for new roles. Because this is the variable's *default*, every consumer of this module who doesn't override ssm_standard_role gets the broader, deprecated policy attached to their bastion's instance role without realising it. No deterministic rule flags this (holden has no policy covering deprecated managed-policy ARNs generically) — see suggested_policies.
findings.title: Default ssm_standard_role points at AWS's deprecated AmazonEC2RoleforSSM managed policy instead of AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore

findings.explanation: data.http.myip fetches `http://ipv4.icanhazip.com` (plain HTTP, unauthenticated). Its response_body is chomped, suffixed with /32, and passed straight through as the module's `allowed_ips` — which becomes the *only* CIDR permitted to reach the bastion's SSH ingress rule (aws_security_group.instance_ssh_access.tf). An on-path attacker (rogue AP, compromised proxy/DNS) can return an arbitrary IP in that plain-HTTP response, which gets baked into the security group as the trusted SSH source instead of the real caller's IP. This requires tracing a value across three files (data source → module call → security group consumer) that the deterministic engine's two-hop graph checks don't cover.
findings.remediation: Use `https://ipv4.icanhazip.com` (TLS-verified) instead of the http:// URL.
findings.title: Example fetches the caller's IP over plain HTTP and feeds it directly into the bastion's sole allowed SSH ingress CIDR

findings.explanation: The caller's workflow-level `permissions:` forms the ceiling for every job inside a called reusable workflow (jobs.<id>.uses:). This is cross-repo composition the deterministic engine has no way to see: I fetched JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-pr.yml directly and it defines three jobs (discover, terraform, security) whose steps are limited to checkout, opentofu setup/init/validate, python setup, and pre-commit — none call the GitHub API to comment on, review, label, or otherwise write to a pull request. This is confirmed empirically, not just by reading the YAML: the last 5 runs of this workflow (e.g. run 25332376226) show exactly those steps executing and nothing PR-write-shaped. `pull-requests: write` is granted to all three jobs but exercised by none of them, so a compromised or newly-added step in any of those jobs would inherit write access to PRs it has no legitimate reason to need.
findings.remediation: Drop `pull-requests: write` from pull_request.yml's top-level permissions, leaving only `contents: read`. If a future step in the reusable workflow needs to post PR comments, re-add it there deliberately.
findings.title: pull_request.yml grants pull-requests: write, but the reusable workflow it calls never uses it

findings.explanation: Fetching JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-verify.yml directly shows four jobs: discover (lists directories, no cloud/write need), terraform (correctly scopes its own `permissions: id-token: write, contents: read` for AWS OIDC auth), security (runs pre-commit, no cloud/write need), and version (correctly scopes `permissions: contents: write` to push a tag). Because discover and security declare no job-level permissions block of their own, they inherit the full caller ceiling (id-token: write, contents: write) from this repo's verify.yml, over-privileging two jobs that only need read access to the checked-out code.
findings.remediation: This can't be fixed from this repo alone — the caller's ceiling is already the minimum needed to cover the terraform and version jobs. The actual fix is in JamesWoolfenden/.github: add explicit `permissions: contents: read` (or an empty `permissions: {}`) to the discover and security jobs in terraform-verify.yml so they don't inherit more than they use, regardless of what any individual caller grants.
findings.title: verify.yml's id-token/contents:write ceiling is inherited by the reusable workflow's discover and security jobs, which don't need either

suggested_policies.rationale: AmazonEC2RoleforSSM is a well-documented AWS deprecation with a specific, unambiguous replacement (AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore). Any Terraform attaching this exact managed-policy ARN via aws_iam_role_policy_attachment (or the aws_iam_role.managed_policy_arns list) is over-provisioning relative to current AWS guidance, regardless of the surrounding module. coverage_by_type[aws_iam_role_policy_attachment] only has HLD_AWS_181 (AdministratorAccess) and HLD_AWS_237 (IAMFullAccess) — no existing policy covers this ARN. Verified: fires correctly on aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.ssm_standard in this repo and nowhere else.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_001
name: IAM role policy attachments must not use the deprecated AmazonEC2RoleforSSM managed policy
principle: identity-and-access
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  AWS deprecated the AmazonEC2RoleforSSM managed policy in favor of
  AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, which grants a narrower, purpose-built
  permission set for the SSM agent. AmazonEC2RoleforSSM bundles broader,
  now-unnecessary permissions that were split out of the core policy.
  Continuing to attach the legacy policy over-provisions the instance role
  relative to what the SSM agent actually requires today.
remediation: |
  Attach arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore instead:

    resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "ssm" {
      role       = aws_iam_role.example.name
      policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore"
    }
resources:
  aws_iam_role_policy_attachment:
    path: policy_arn
    not_equals: "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AmazonEC2RoleforSSM"

suggested_policies.rationale: data.http with a non-https URL is a concrete, single-attribute, broadly-applicable check — any Terraform using the http provider's data source is subject to it, independent of how the response is later used. coverage_by_type[data.http] is empty (zero existing policies). Verified: fires correctly on data.http.myip in example/examplea and nowhere else in the repo.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_002
name: data.http data sources must use an https:// URL
principle: encryption
severity: MEDIUM
rationale: |
  A data "http" source fetching over a plain http:// URL has no transport
  integrity or confidentiality guarantee. Any on-path attacker can alter the
  response body, and Terraform configurations frequently feed that response
  directly into security-relevant values (allowlisted CIDRs, endpoint URLs,
  bootstrap scripts) without further validation, silently trusting whatever
  the attacker returns.
remediation: |
  Use an https:// URL instead:

    data "http" "example" {
      url = "https://example.com"
    }
resources:
  data.http:
    path: url
    matches: "^https://"

suggested_policies.dsl_extension_note: Need a per-element regex operator for list-valued string attributes, e.g. `list_any_matches: <regex>` (pass when at least one element of the list at `path` matches the Go regex) as a sibling to the existing `contains` (exact membership) and `matches` (whole-string) operators. Evaluator shape: new case in the same dispatch switch as `matches`/`contains` in internal/policy/evaluator.go, resolving `path` to a []string then regexp.MatchString per element.
suggested_policies.rationale: IAM statements granting ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey with a Resource ending in instance/* (rather than specific instance ARNs or a tag-scoped Condition) is a recurring, real-world Instance Connect misconfiguration — not specific to this account or org. coverage_by_type[data.aws_iam_policy_document] is empty, and HLD_AWS_222 (no-wildcard-resource) only matches a literal "*" element, not a suffix pattern like instance/*, so it does not overlap. Expressing this precisely requires evaluating each element of a list-valued attribute (resources) against a regex, which the current DSL's contains (exact-value membership) and matches (whole-string) operators don't support together in one condition.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_PROPOSED_003
name: IAM policy statements should not grant ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey on all instances via a instance/* resource pattern
principle: identity-and-access
severity: HIGH
rationale: |
  A statement granting ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey with a resource
  ending in instance/* (with no more specific instance ARN and no
  aws:ResourceTag condition scoping which instances) lets any principal with
  this permission push an SSH public key onto every EC2 instance in the
  account/region that has the matching OS user, not just the intended target.
  This converts what looks like scoped bastion access into account-wide
  lateral SSH reach.
remediation: |
  Scope the resource to specific instance ARNs, or add a Condition such as
  aws:ResourceTag/<tag-key> restricting which instances the key can be sent
  to:

    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "aws:ResourceTag/Name"
      values   = ["my-bastion"]
    }
resources:
  data.aws_iam_policy_document:
    path: statement
    not_any:
      all:
        - path: actions
          contains: "ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey"
        - path: resources
          list_any_matches: "instance/\\*$"
